title: Aman, the Blessed Realm
blurb: Aman is the western land across the Great Sea where the Valar settled and where the Elves later lived in light.
book:
Aman lies far to the west of Middle-earth, across the Great Sea called Belegaer. The name means blessed, free from evil. Melkor lived there for a time after his release and sowed lies among the Noldor. The great harm came when he and Ungoliant killed the Two Trees.

The Valar left Almaren after Melkor destroyed the Lamps. They made their home in Aman and raised the Pelóri, a great wall of mountains, near its eastern shore. Eldamar, or Elvenhome, is the land of the Elves by that shore and in its bay. The Elves who answered the summons lived there.

The Akallabêth says the land itself does not make mortals deathless. It is deathless because the Valar dwell there, and a mortal there would only wither sooner. After the Noldor rebelled and left, the Valar set the Shadowy Seas and the Enchanted Isles in the sea to the east to guard it.

When Númenor fell, Aman was taken out of the round world. Only the Straight Road leads there now. Elves may sail it, and a few others were allowed by special grace. The Ring-bearers passed over the Sea at the end of the Third Age.

facts.Guarded by: The Pelóri and the Enchanted Isles

places.note: The Grey Havens is the gate from which ships took the Straight Road to Aman.

sources: The Silmarillion, Valaquenta and Quenta Silmarillion; Akallabêth

title: Valinor
kind: Realm of the Valar in Aman
blurb: Valinor is the part of Aman where the Valar built their cities and where the Two Trees gave light before the Sun.
book:
Valinor is the land of the Valar inside Aman, west of the Pelóri mountains. It lies far west of every land on the maps. The Valar made their dwellings here after leaving Almaren.

At the green mound Ezellohar, outside the city of Valmar, Yavanna sang the Two Trees into growth. Telperion gave silver light and Laurelin gave gold. This age is called the Days of Bliss, and the Elves who came to Valinor lived in its light.

The Valar had halls of their own, such as the mansions of Mandos and the gardens of Lórien and Yavanna. The Vanyar, and for a time the Noldor, lived near the mountains.

Melkor and Ungoliant killed the Trees, and the Noldor under Fëanor left Valinor to hunt Morgoth. Yavanna saved a last flower and a last fruit. From these the Valar made the Moon and the Sun.

The Valar withdrew behind guarded seas. After the fall of Númenor, Valinor could no longer be reached by an ordinary road.

facts.Direction: West, in Aman beyond the Great Sea
facts.Light: Telperion and Laurelin, until Melkor and Ungoliant killed them

sources: The Silmarillion, Valaquenta; Quenta Silmarillion, chapters 1 to 9

title: Taniquetil and Valmar
kind: Mountain and city of the Valar
blurb: Taniquetil is the highest mountain of the world and Manwë's seat. Valmar is the Valar's city of many bells.
book:
Taniquetil is the tallest mountain in the world. It rises in the Pelóri in the east of Valinor, near the coast, and its peak is always white. The Elves also call it Oiolossë.

Manwë and Varda keep their halls on the summit. From there Manwë looks over the whole world, and Varda hears the cries of those who call on her name, Elbereth, from Middle-earth.

Valmar lies on the plain of Valinor, west of the mountains. It is the city of the Valar, and it has many bells. The mound Ezellohar stands by its western gate, and the Two Trees grew there.

The Vanyar, the first kindred of the Elves to come to Valinor, lived on the slopes of Taniquetil and in Valmar, near Manwë. The Valar met in council at Máhanaxar, the Ring of Doom, outside the gates of Valmar.

Nothing in the books places these sites on any map of Middle-earth. They lie across the Great Sea in the far west.
sources: The Silmarillion, Valaquenta and Quenta Silmarillion, chapters 1 and 3

title: Tirion upon Túna
blurb: Tirion is the white Elven city on the hill Túna, where the Noldor lived before the Exile.
book:
Tirion stands on the green hill Túna, in the gap of the Pelóri known as the Calacirya. It faces the sea, far west of the lands on the maps.

The Noldor and the Vanyar first built it together. Later the Vanyar moved into Valinor to live near Manwë, and the Noldor kept the city. Finwë was their king.

A tall white tower called Mindon Eldaliéva stood in the city. Its lamp could be seen far out to sea.

Tirion was the home of Fëanor and his kin, and the place where his quarrel with his half-brother Fingolfin grew. When the Valar banished Fëanor to Formenos, Finwë went with him, and Fingolfin ruled the Noldor in Tirion.

After Morgoth killed Finwë, most of the Noldor left Valinor. Finarfin turned back after the Doom of Mandos, and he ruled the Noldor who remained in Tirion.
sources: The Silmarillion, Quenta Silmarillion, chapters 3 and 6 to 9

title: Alqualondë
kind: Haven of the Teleri in Aman
blurb: Alqualondë is the Teleri port in Aman, where the first Kinslaying took place.
book:
Alqualondë is a harbour city on the coast of Eldamar in Aman, west of the lands on the maps. The Teleri built it after they crossed the Sea. It lies in a bay with an arch of rock that guards the harbour mouth.

Olwë ruled the city. The Teleri loved ships and the sea, and they built swan-shaped ships with the help of Ossë. They also made lamps that lit the harbour.

When Fëanor decided to leave for Middle-earth, he asked the Teleri for their ships. They refused. Fëanor's Noldor then attacked the city and killed many Teleri, and took the ships. This is the first Kinslaying. The Teleri lost many people, and Tolkien says the Noldor suffered under the Doom of Mandos as a result.

Ossë and Uinen were friends of the Teleri, and Uinen wept for the slain mariners. Olwë was the brother of Thingol, King of Doriath.

The ships that Fëanor took crossed to Middle-earth, and he burned them at Losgar.

facts.Event: First Kinslaying, at the Darkening of Valinor

sources: The Silmarillion, Quenta Silmarillion, chapters 5 and 9

title: Tol Eressëa and Avallónë
blurb: Tol Eressëa is an island off Aman where the Teleri lived, and Avallónë is its port.
book:
Tol Eressëa is a large island in the Bay of Eldamar, west of Middle-earth and near the coast of Aman. Ulmo drew it across the Sea like a great ship, to carry the Teleri to Aman. Ossë later rooted it to the floor of the bay.

The Teleri lived there for a long age and learned the songs of the sea. Later they moved to the mainland, where they built Alqualondë. Some Elves stayed on the island.

Avallónë is its haven. The name is linked to the nearness of the island to Valinor. After the First Age, Elves of Tol Eressëa became friends of the Númenóreans and sailed to Númenor with gifts. The Númenóreans cherished a tree from Tol Eressëa.

At the Drowning of Númenor, Aman and Tol Eressëa were both taken out of the circles of the world. Only the Straight Road leads to them now. In letters, Tolkien says that the Ring-bearers went to Tol Eressëa.

Many Elves lived there in the Third Age and after.

facts.Direction: West, in the Bay of Eldamar

sources: The Silmarillion, Quenta Silmarillion, chapters 5 and 20; Akallabêth; Letters

title: The Pelóri and the Calacirya
kind: Mountain wall and pass of Aman
blurb: The Pelóri are the great mountain wall around Valinor, and the Calacirya is its only gap.
book:
The Pelóri are a chain of mountains that the Valar raised along the east side of Aman. They lie on the far side of the Great Sea from Middle-earth. The Valar built them after Melkor destroyed the Lamps, to keep Valinor safe from him.

Taniquetil is the highest peak of the Pelóri. The mountains are steep and cold on their outer side. The strip of land between them and the sea is Eldamar.

The Calacirya, or Pass of Light, is a great cleft in the middle of the Pelóri. Light from the Two Trees poured through it onto the shore beyond. The green hill Túna stands in the gap, and Tirion is built on it. The Elves of Eldamar lived near it, and they could look out to sea in the light.

The pass was the only break in the mountain wall. The Akallabêth tells that Ar-Pharazôn landed on the shore of Aman, and Númenor was destroyed soon after.

facts.Raised: After the fall of the Lamps

sources: The Silmarillion, Quenta Silmarillion, chapters 1, 3 and 5; Akallabêth

title: The Helcaraxë
kind: Frozen strait between Aman and Middle-earth
blurb: The Helcaraxë is the icy strait in the far north where Fingolfin's host crossed from Aman to Middle-earth.
book:
The Helcaraxë lies in the far north, where Aman comes close to the lands of Middle-earth. Ice fills the narrow sea, and it grinds and breaks in the cold. This gave it the name Grinding Ice.

After Fëanor took the Teleri ships and burned them at Losgar, Fingolfin and his people had no ships. They had to choose between returning to the Valar and crossing the ice. Pride and loyalty to their kin drove them to go on.

The crossing cost the Noldor many lives. Some fell into the water and some died of cold. Among those lost was Elenwë, wife of Turgon. Fingolfin's host included Fingon, Turgon, Finrod, Galadriel and their followers.

They reached Middle-earth when the Moon first rose. The long journey left bitterness between the two houses.

The strait lies in the far north, between Araman on the coast of Aman and the northern shores of Middle-earth. Nothing in the books tells us what became of the Helcaraxë after the Change of the World.

facts.Direction: Far north, between Araman and Middle-earth
facts.Crossed by: Fingolfin's host, arriving at the first rising of the Moon

sources: The Silmarillion, Quenta Silmarillion, chapters 9 to 11

title: Almaren and the Two Lamps
blurb: Almaren was the first home of the Valar on an island in a lake, lit by two great lamps until Melkor destroyed them.
book:
Almaren was the first dwelling of the Valar in Arda, in the centre of Middle-earth. It stood on an island in a great lake. It lies far from the north-west lands on the maps, and its position is known only in the old tales.

Aulë made two great lamps to light the world. Illuin stood in the north and Ormal stood in the south. Their light fell over all the land, and this time is called the Spring of Arda. Plants and creatures grew in the light.

Melkor returned in secret while the Valar rested. He built the fortress Utumno in the north, and then he threw down both pillars of the Lamps. The fall of the Lamps shattered the shape of the world, and fire and water flooded the land. Almaren was destroyed.

The Valar left Middle-earth and went west to Aman, where they made Valinor. Tolkien notes that the lamps' fall also changed the seas and mountains.

The books give no later account of the island.
sources: The Silmarillion, Quenta Silmarillion, chapters 1 and 3

title: Utumno
blurb: Utumno was Melkor's first great fortress, in the far north of Middle-earth, broken in the War of the Powers.
book:
Utumno was a great fortress of Melkor in the far north of Middle-earth. It lay far beyond the lands of the Third Age and of Beleriand. Melkor delved it in secret while the Valar dwelt on Almaren, and from it he went out to throw down the Lamps.

From Utumno Melkor ruled his servants and bred evil creatures. He hunted the first Elves who woke at Cuiviénen. Sauron was his chief servant.

The Valar waged the War of the Powers to free the Elves. They marched into the north and besieged Utumno. The war was long. The north of Middle-earth was changed, and the Great Sea between Aman and Middle-earth grew wide and deep. Tulkas wrestled Melkor down, and the Valar bound him and carried him to Aman.

Melkor's second stronghold, Angband, was not fully searched. Sauron was not found, and many evil things lingered there. When Melkor fled from Valinor, he returned to Angband and built it anew.

The books do not tell of Utumno after the war.

facts.Fall: War of the Powers, before the Sun

sources: The Silmarillion, Quenta Silmarillion, chapters 1, 3 and 4

title: Cuiviénen
blurb: Cuiviénen is the bay in the far east of Middle-earth where the first Elves woke under the stars.
book:
Cuiviénen means Water of Awakening. It was a bay of an inland sea in the far east of Middle-earth. It lies far beyond every map of the Third Age.

The first Elves woke beside it under the stars, before the Sun and Moon. They called themselves the Quendi, those who speak with voices.

Melkor hunted them from Utumno. Oromë found the Elves while riding in the east, and the Valar summoned them to Valinor. Many set out on the Great Journey west, and some refused.

Those who refused are the Avari, the Unwilling. Those who went became the Eldar: the Vanyar, the Noldor and the Teleri. The Sindar were Teleri who stayed in Beleriand and never crossed the Sea.

The Silmarillion places Cuiviénen by the Sea of Helcar, which filled the place where the Lamp Illuin had stood. Later writings outside the published books name the first Elf-fathers, but The Silmarillion does not. The books do not say what became of the shore.
sources: The Silmarillion, Quenta Silmarillion, chapters 3 and 4

title: Hildórien
blurb: Hildórien is the land in the far east where the first Men woke at the first sunrise.
book:
Hildórien is the land in the east of Middle-earth where Men first woke. They woke at the first rising of the Sun. The Elves called Men the Hildor, the Followers, because they came after the Elves, and the name of the land comes from this.

The Valar did not come to guide Men or summon them to Valinor. The books say little of their first days. The Silmarillion hints that Morgoth went among them and that a darkness lay on their early history.

Some Men wandered west. The first of them to reach Beleriand were the people of Bëor, more than three hundred years after the Noldor came there. Finrod Felagund found them in Ossiriand. Bëor told him that a darkness lay behind them in the east, and that they had turned their backs on it.

The books give no firm location for Hildórien beyond the eastern lands. Nothing is told of what became of it.

facts.Event: Awakening of Men at the first sunrise
facts.Name: From Hildor, the Followers

sources: The Silmarillion, Quenta Silmarillion, chapters 11, 12 and 17

title: Númenor
blurb: Númenor was the great island west of Middle-earth given to the Edain, which sank in S.A. 3319.
book:
Númenor was an island raised from the sea by the Valar and given to the Edain who fought against Morgoth. It lay far to the west in the Great Sea. The Edain called it Elenna, Starwards, because Eärendil's star guided them to it. It was also called Andor, the Land of Gift.

It had the shape of a five-pointed star. The Meneltarma rose in the middle. Forostar lay in the north, Andustar in the west and Mittalmar inland. Hyarnustar lay in the south-west, Hyarrostar in the south-east and Orrostar in the east. Arandor was the kingsland.

Elros was the first king, in S.A. 32. The Númenóreans lived long and sailed far. They founded havens in Middle-earth, including Umbar.

In time the Kings grew proud and feared death. Ar-Pharazôn took Sauron captive, and Sauron corrupted him. The king sailed to Aman with a fleet. Eru broke the world, and Númenor sank in S.A. 3319.

Elendil and his people escaped and founded Arnor and Gondor.
sources: The Silmarillion, Akallabêth; Unfinished Tales, The Description of the Island of Númenor

title: Armenelos
blurb: Armenelos was the royal city of Númenor, with the palace, the court of the White Tree and, later, the Temple of Melkor.
book:
Armenelos was the royal city of Númenor. It stood in Arandor, the King's land, in the middle part of the island. It was the seat of the Kings for most of Númenor's history.

The palace of the Kings stood there. Nimloth, the White Tree, grew in the King's court. The tombs of the Kings did not lie in the city but in a valley at the foot of the Meneltarma.

Ar-Pharazôn built the Temple of Melkor in the city. It had a great dome. Sauron, who had been brought as a captive, became the King's counsellor. Men were sacrificed in the Temple, according to the Akallabêth.

Sauron urged the King to cut down Nimloth. Isildur went in secret into the court and took a fruit from the tree. Later the King yielded, and the tree was felled and burned in the Temple. From the fruit came the line of the White Tree of Gondor.

Armenelos was destroyed in the drowning of the island in S.A. 3319.

facts.Features: Palace, King's court with Nimloth, Temple of Melkor

sources: The Silmarillion, Akallabêth; Unfinished Tales, A Description of the Island of Númenor

title: Rómenna
blurb: Rómenna was the great eastern port of Númenor, facing Middle-earth, and the home of Elendil's line.
book:
Rómenna was a harbour on the east coast of Númenor. It faced Middle-earth, and it was the main port for ships heading east. It lay far from the mapped lands, across the Great Sea.

Tar-Aldarion, the sixth King, loved the sea. His ships sailed from the east coast to Middle-earth, and he became a friend of Gil-galad in Lindon.

In the later days many of the Faithful were moved to the east of the island, and Rómenna became their chief home. Elendil, son of Amandil, was of the line of Elros and lived in Rómenna with his sons Isildur and Anárion.

When Sauron came to Númenor, the Faithful were hated. Elendil gathered ships in the harbour. His fleet left at the time of the Downfall. He reached Middle-earth and founded the realms of Arnor and Gondor.

The city sank with the island in S.A. 3319.
sources: The Silmarillion, Akallabêth; Unfinished Tales, Aldarion and Erendis

title: Andúnië
blurb: Andúnië was the western port of Númenor, home of the Lords of Andúnië, who stayed loyal to the Valar.
book:
Andúnië was a harbour on the west coast of Númenor. It faced Aman across the sea. The Númenóreans looked west from there to Tol Eressëa.

The Lords of Andúnië were a great house of Númenor. They descended from Silmariën, a child of King Tar-Elendil. They were friendly with the Elves and remained Faithful to the Valar.

Amandil was the last Lord. He was a friend of the Elves. When Ar-Pharazôn made war on the Valar, Amandil tried to warn the Faithful. He sailed west in secret, hoping to ask the Valar for mercy. He did not return.

His son Elendil gathered ships at Rómenna and fled to Middle-earth with his sons.

In the early days Elvish ships from Eressëa came to Andúnië with gifts. As the Kings turned from the Valar, the Elves came seldom and in secret, and at last they no longer came.

Andúnië sank with Númenor in S.A. 3319.
sources: The Silmarillion, Akallabêth; Unfinished Tales

title: The Meneltarma
blurb: The Meneltarma was the tall mountain at the centre of Númenor, where the Kings prayed to Eru.
book:
The Meneltarma, or Pillar of Heaven, stood in the middle of Númenor. It was the only high mountain on the island. It lay far west of the lands on the maps.

The Númenóreans held its summit as the Hallow of Eru. They built no temple on it. Three times each year the King went up to give prayer and thanks to Eru Ilúvatar, and many of the people followed him. At all times silence was kept there.

Tolkien says the Kings kept the custom in honour of Eru, who had given the island to the Edain.

In the later days the Kings neglected the prayers. Under Ar-Pharazôn no one might climb the mountain, on pain of death. Sauron persuaded the King to build a Temple to Melkor at Armenelos instead. The people no longer prayed on the mountain.

When Ar-Pharazôn landed in Aman, the fleet was destroyed and the island sank. Fire burst from the Meneltarma as the land went down, and the mountain was lost with the island.

facts.Use: Holy place for prayer to Eru

sources: The Silmarillion, Akallabêth; Unfinished Tales

title: Harad, Near and Far
blurb: Harad is the wide southern region beyond Gondor and Mordor, home of the Haradrim and of Men of many peoples.
book:
Harad means the South. It lies south of Gondor and of Mordor, beyond the river Harnen. Only its northern edge appears on the Middle-earth map.

Near Harad is the nearer part. The Haradrim fought against Gondor many times, and their kings often allied with Sauron. Umbar, on the coast, was long contested between Gondor and the Men of the South.

Far Harad lies farther south. Men from there fought at the Pelennor Fields, and the book describes them as black and huge. The Haradrim brought the great beasts called mûmakil, or oliphaunts, to war.

In the War of the Ring, Southrons marched with Sauron's armies to Gondor. Faramir's men ambushed a company of them in Ithilien. Their chief at the Pelennor fought under a black serpent on a scarlet banner, and Théoden slew him.

The people of Harad had many tongues and lords. The books do not describe their cities or customs in detail.

After the fall of Sauron, King Elessar made peace with the peoples of Harad.

places.note: The map shows only the northern edge of Harad.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A and B; The Two Towers, Book IV, chapter 4; The Return of the King, Book V, chapter 6, and Book VI, chapter 5

title: Umbar
blurb: Umbar is the great natural harbour south of Gondor, held in turn by Númenóreans, Gondor and the Corsairs.
book:
Umbar is a large natural harbour on the coast of the South, a long sail south of Gondor. It lies beyond the Bay of Belfalas, past Harondor.

The Númenóreans made it a great haven in the Second Age. After the Downfall, Black Númenóreans who served Sauron held it. Gondor took it under King Eärnil I in T.A. 933.

After the Kin-strife (T.A. 1432 to 1448), the rebels who had followed Castamir the Usurper fled to Umbar. They became the Corsairs of Umbar and raided the coasts of Gondor for centuries. King Telumehtar took Umbar back in T.A. 1810 and took the name Umbardacil. Later it was lost again to the Men of Harad.

In T.A. 2980 Aragorn, serving Gondor under the name Thorongil, led a raid on Umbar and burned many Corsair ships.

During the War of the Ring, a Corsair fleet sailed up the Anduin against Gondor. Aragorn captured it at Pelargir with the help of the Dead Men, and sailed it to Minas Tirith.

The books do not say what became of the haven after the War of the Ring.

facts.Direction: South of Gondor, beyond the Bay of Belfalas

places.note: The Corsair fleet of Umbar sailed up the Anduin to Pelargir.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (I, iv) and Appendix B; The Return of the King, Book V, chapter 9

title: Khand
blurb: Khand is a land south-east of Mordor whose warriors, the Variags, served Sauron against Gondor.
book:
Khand lies south-east of Mordor. The general map of The Lord of the Rings shows its name in that corner, and the books tell almost nothing more about it.

Its people are the Variags. The Return of the King names the Variags of Khand among the enemies who came to the Battle of the Pelennor Fields. They fought there beside Easterlings and Southrons in Sauron's host.

Appendix A tells that in T.A. 1944 the Wainriders made an alliance with the Men of Khand and of Near Harad. Together they attacked Gondor from the north and from the south. King Ondoher fell in that war, but Eärnil defeated the southern army and then the Wainriders.

The books give no names of towns or kings of Khand. They say nothing of its customs or of its later history. Any fuller picture of the land is a reader's invention.

facts.Wars: Allies of the Wainriders, T.A. 1944; Pelennor Fields, T.A. 3019

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (I, iv); The Return of the King, Book V, chapter 6; general map

title: Dorwinion
kind: Wine-land by the Sea of Rhûn
blurb: Dorwinion is a land in the east known for its strong wine, which reached the Elvenking of Mirkwood.
book:
Dorwinion is a land in the east of Middle-earth. The Hobbit names it as the source of a strong wine. The maps in the books do not show it.

In The Hobbit, the Elvenking of Mirkwood drinks wine from Dorwinion. The wine reached his halls by trade, and empty barrels were floated back down the Forest River to Lake-town. The chief guard and the butler drank the wine and fell asleep, and Bilbo took the keys. He and the Dwarves then escaped in empty barrels.

The book gives no names of towns or kings in Dorwinion, and says almost nothing of its people.

A map that Tolkien annotated for the artist Pauline Baynes places Dorwinion on the north-west shore of the Sea of Rhûn. That map is not part of the books.

The books tell nothing of its later history.

facts.Direction: East; placed by the Sea of Rhûn only on the Baynes map

places.note: A map Tolkien annotated places Dorwinion on the shore of the Sea of Rhûn.

sources: The Hobbit, chapter 9; Tolkien's notes on the Pauline Baynes map

title: The far East and South of Middle-earth
kind: What the books say of distant lands
blurb: The books say very little of the far East and South, apart from a few peoples, beasts and names.
book:
Tolkien made maps of the north-west only, and he told little of the rest of Middle-earth. The books mention the East and South mainly through the peoples who came from there to war.

In the East, beyond Rhûn, live the Easterlings. Many of them served Sauron and fought against Gondor. Khand, home of the Variags, lies south-east of Mordor. Unfinished Tales says that two of the five Wizards went into the East and did not return. Tolkien guessed about them in letters but settled nothing.

In the South, beyond Near Harad, lies Far Harad. Men from there came to the Pelennor Fields, and the Haradrim brought mûmakil, the great oliphaunts, to Gondor's wars.

Appendix A says that Aragorn journeyed far into Rhûn and Harad, under stars he did not know. The books do not tell what he saw there.

The maps of the Third Age fade out beyond these lands. Sauron's power reached far into the East and South, but the books do not map his realms there.

Because the books give so little, any detailed picture of the far East and South goes beyond what Tolkien wrote.
sources: The Lord of the Rings, Book V, chapter 6; Appendix A (The Tale of Aragorn and Arwen)
Unfinished Tales, The Istari
Tolkien, Letters, no. 211

title: The Straight Road and the bending of the world
kind: How Aman left the circles of the world
blurb: The Straight Road is the Elves' sea-path to Aman, left open when the Valar bent the world after Númenor sank.
book:
Before Númenor fell, a mortal could sail west to Aman, because the world was flat. When Ar-Pharazôn landed there, Manwë called on Eru. Eru changed the world.

The world was made round. Aman and Tol Eressëa were removed from the circles of the world. A mortal who sails west now returns to his starting point and finds no end to the sea.

The Straight Road remains. It runs from the western coasts of Middle-earth to the land of the Valar. Only Elves, and others who are allowed, can follow it. For them, the road passes over the bending of the world. It is hidden from mortal sight.

Ships of the Elves left from the Grey Havens to the Straight Road in the Third Age and after. Círdan kept the ships there. Elrond, Galadriel, Gandalf, Bilbo and Frodo went there when the Third Age ended.

After this, Aman and its lands could not be reached by an ordinary voyage.

facts.Event: The Changing of the World, S.A. 3319

places.note: Ships of the Elves left the Grey Havens for the Straight Road.

sources: The Silmarillion, Akallabêth; The Lord of the Rings, Book VI, chapter 9

title: The Void and the Doors of Night
blurb: The Void is the emptiness outside the world, and the Door of Night is the gate through which Morgoth was thrust.
book:
Arda is enclosed by the Walls of the World, and beyond them lies the Void, the empty space outside the world. The Silmarillion does not say where the Door of Night stands. No mapped place lies near it.

Before the world was made, Melkor often went alone into the void places, seeking the Imperishable Flame. He did not find it, for it is with Ilúvatar.

After the War of Wrath, the Valar thrust Morgoth through the Door of Night beyond the Walls of the World, into the Timeless Void. A guard is set on those walls, and Eärendil keeps watch in the sky on Vingilot with the Silmaril.

The lies that Morgoth sowed still bore fruit after he was gone, as the last chapter of the Quenta Silmarillion says.

Drafts that are not in the published books tell of his return at a Last Battle. The Silmarillion itself does not tell this, and Tolkien did not describe the Void any further.

facts.Place: Outside the Walls of the World

title: What survived the drowning of Beleriand
kind: Remnants of the First Age lands
blurb: After the War of Wrath most of Beleriand sank. Lindon and a few isles, such as Himling, Tol Fuin and Tol Morwen, remained.
book:
At the end of the First Age, the War of Wrath broke the north-west of Middle-earth. The sea rushed in, and most of Beleriand was drowned. The books name only a few pieces that remained.

Part of Ossiriand, west of the Ered Luin, stayed above the water and kept the name Lindon. Gil-galad ruled there, and Círdan kept the Grey Havens. The sea broke through the mountains and made the Gulf of Lune, which split Lindon in two.

The general map of The Lord of the Rings shows two isles off the coast. Himling keeps the name of the hill of Himring, where Maedhros had his fortress. Tol Fuin is a remnant of the highlands of Dorthonion, which were called Taur-nu-Fuin after their fall.

The Silmarillion adds Tol Morwen. The stone over the grave of Túrin and Morwen stood above the waters as a lonely isle.

Tolkien drew no full map of the new coasts, so the shape of what survived is not fully known. The rest of Beleriand, with Doriath, Nargothrond and Gondolin, lay under the sea.

facts.Survived: Lindon, Himling, Tol Fuin and Tol Morwen
facts.Cause: War of Wrath, end of the First Age

places.note: Lindon is the main land that survived.

The hill of Himring became the isle of Himling.
Tol Fuin is a remnant of these highlands.
